content.content:
1	# DevDesk Backlog
2	
3	**Last Updated:** 2026-08-02
4	
5	Open work for DevDesk: known defects, technical debt, and planned features.
6	Replaces the former `todo.md` at the repository root. Items completed there
7	(network topology visualisation, inter-container ping/curl) have been dropped
8	rather than carried over.
9	
10	---
11	
12	## 1. Known defects
13	
14	D1, D3 and D6 (the byte-vs-rune lot), then D2, D5 and D7, were fixed; see
15	[§1.1](#11-fixed). **D4 is the only one left**, and it is waiting on a decision
16	rather than on work.
17	
18	### D4 — `DeleteConfirmModal` uses `Tab` for field navigation
19	
20	`internal/ui/components/delete_confirm_modal.go:89-97`
21	
22	`tab` / `shift+tab` cycle checkbox → Yes → No. Rule 135 reserves those keys for
23	tab switching and assigns field navigation to `↑ / ↓` exclusively.
24	
25	Cosmetic in isolation, but it is the kind of inconsistency Rule 135 exists to
26	prevent. Changing it alters muscle memory, so it needs a deliberate call rather
27	than a drive-by fix.
28	
29	Note that the surrounding code moved when D2 was fixed: `tab` / `shift+tab` now
30	cycle through `cycleFocus()`, which skips the locked checkbox. Switching to
31	`↑ / ↓` remains a one-line change to the key names.
32	
33	### D8 — Write-only CRUD flags and an unreachable handler in the status view
34	
35	`internal/ui/status/model.go:64-67` and `internal/ui/status/update.go:57-60`
36	
37	`Model.creating`, `Model.editing` and `Model.confirming` are assigned in five
38	places and read in none: the view keys off `componentForm != nil` and
39	`confirmModal != nil` instead. `HasActiveForm`, the one method that read them, is
40	commented out at `model.go:139`.
41	
42	`ComponentFormCancelledMsg` is never sent either. `ComponentForm.handleKeyMsg`
43	answers `esc` by returning a nil form, and the caller stores that — so the
44	`case components.ComponentFormCancelledMsg` branch in `Update()` cannot run. Its
45	body is the only thing that would reset `creating` / `editing`, which is why they
46	would stay true after a cancellation if anything did read them.
47	
48	Harmless today, but it is state that lies: a reader reasonably assumes those
49	flags mean something. Found while writing the phase 2 tests; the tests
50	deliberately assert on `componentForm` / `confirmModal` rather than on the flags,
51	so removing them breaks nothing.
52	
53	**Fix:** delete the three fields, the unreachable case and the message type — or
54	give `esc` a message and make the flags load-bearing. Deleting is the smaller
55	change and matches how the view already works.
56	
57	### D9 — The containers list opens sorted Z→A
58	
59	`internal/ui/containers/model.go:140-147`
60	
61	`New()` sets neither `sortColumn` nor `sortAsc`, so both take their zero value:
62	name, *descending*. The status view, which has the same cycle-sort mechanism,
63	sets `sortAsc: true` explicitly. The header does show `Name ▼`, so the view is
64	at least honest about it — but nobody chose it, and it disagrees with the other
65	list view in the application.
66	
67	**Fix:** set `sortAsc: true` in `New()`, one line. Left for a deliberate call
68	because it changes what the user sees on open.
69	`TestDefaultSortIsNameDescending` pins the current behaviour and says so.
70	
71	### 1.1 Fixed
72	
73	**Two views' help advertised keys that do nothing.** Found while writing the
74	phase 2 tests, not previously recorded.
75	
76	The status view's `GetHelpContent` documented `n` for "Add a new monitor" while
77	the binding has been `ctrl+n` since Rule 111 standardised it, and the `/` filter
78	was missing altogether; the empty-state message told the user to "Press [n]" too.
79	The containers view advertised `S` (shell in a new window) in `GetShortcuts()`
80	without documenting it at all.
81	
82	The workspaces view had it too, found in phase 3: `n` and `Enter` documented
83	where the bindings are `ctrl+n` and `enter`, `/` undocumented, and the same
84	stale "Press [n]" in its empty state.
85	
86	All three are fixed, and each package now asserts that every key
87	`GetShortcuts()` advertises appears in `GetHelpContent()` — the check that would
88	have caught the drift when it was introduced. Three views in a row carried it,
89	so assume `explorer` and `security` do as well.
90	
91	**A stranded cursor in the workspaces table.** `bubbles/table.SetRows` does not
92	clamp the cursor when the row count shrinks. Drilling into a directory with
93	fewer entries — or narrowing the filter — left the cursor past the end: nothing
94	highlighted, and `enter`, `ctrl+d`, `r` and `ctrl+s` all silently did nothing
95	until the user pressed an arrow key. `updateTableData` now clamps.
96	
97	The containers view avoids this by calling `GotoTop()` after every filter
98	change; workspaces had no equivalent. Worth checking in `explorer`, which has
99	the same drill-down shape.
100	
101	**D7** (`extractTarGz` kept parent references in archive paths), **D2** (the
102	"permanent delete" checkbox was documented as locked but was not) and **D5** (an
103	unreachable focus clamp in `CreationForm`) were fixed together — three small,
104	independent defects with no shared code.
105	
106	`extractTarGz` now routes every member name through `sanitizeArchivePath`, which
107	normalises the separators and rejects anything resolving outside the root.
108	Cleaning happens *after* the leading separator is stripped, not before:
109	`path.Clean("/../x")` returns `"/x"`, which would have absorbed the traversal
110	silently instead of exposing it. Traversal that resolves back inside the root
111	(`templates/../README.md`) is kept, normalised. Backslashes are folded to `/`
112	first, so `..\..\etc\passwd` cannot pass as an ordinary filename on a tar reader
113	that treats it as one.
114	
115	The delete modal carries a `locked` flag, set only by
116	`NewDeleteConfirmModalPermanent`. Rather than merely making the toggle a no-op,
117	navigation skips the checkbox entirely (`minFocus()` / `cycleFocus()`) and the
118	line renders dimmed: a focusable control that ignores every key is more
119	confusing than one that is plainly not there.
120	
121	The `CreationForm` clamp was deleted and replaced by a comment recording why it
122	cannot fire, so it is not reintroduced defensively. A test pins the invariant it
123	was guarding.
124	
125	Both self-annulling tests became real assertions:
126	`TestDeleteConfirmModalPermanentCheckboxIsStillToggleable` →
127	`TestDeleteConfirmModalPermanentCheckboxIsLocked` (plus navigation and
128	confirmation cases), and `TestExtractTarGzPreservesParentTraversalInKeys` →
129	`TestExtractTarGzRejectsParentTraversal` (table-driven over five escape shapes)
130	alongside `TestExtractTarGzNormalisesContainedTraversal`.
131	
132	**D1** (`ReportModal.View()` emitted invalid UTF-8), **D3** (`wrapInputLines`
133	looped forever when `wrapWidth <= 0`) and **D6** (`wordWrap` measured bytes) were
134	fixed together, since D1 and D6 were the same byte-vs-rune defect.
135	
136	Rather than patch each call site, the truncation logic moved into
137	`internal/ui/theme/text.go` per Rule 117: `StringWidth`, `TruncateWidth` (keeps
138	the head) and `TruncateTailWidth` (keeps the tail, for paths). All three measure
139	terminal columns, so double-width glyphs are handled too, not just multibyte
140	ones.
141	
142	A **fourth site carried the same defect** and was not recorded here: `truncate`
143	in `internal/ui/security/model.go` sliced bytes exactly like D1 and rendered
144	Trivy finding titles. It is now `theme.TruncateWidth` and the local helper is
145	gone.
146	
147	A **fifth site** turned up later, during the phase 3 tests: `firstOutputLine` in
148	`internal/ui/netdiag` sliced `line[:maxLen-3]` to fill the Output column of the
149	results table, so any diagnostic whose first line contained a multibyte rune
150	could be cut in half and bleed across the rows below (Rule 122). Now
151	`theme.TruncateWidth`, pinned by `TestFirstOutputLineKeepsMultibyteRunesIntact`.
152	Worth grepping for `[:` on strings when the remaining phases land.
153	
154	The two pinned tests that `t.Skip()`d became real assertions
155	(`TestReportModalViewKeepsMultibyteRunesIntact`,
156	`TestWordWrapMeasuresColumnsNotBytes`).
157	
158	One call site was deliberately left alone: `truncateResultLine` in
159	`internal/ui/oci_resources/connectivity_form.go` counts runes rather than bytes,
160	so it is correct — merely imprecise on double-width glyphs. Folding it into the
161	theme helpers is a cleanup, not a defect fix.
162	
163	**Context isolation in `GitCredentialStorage` never worked.** Found while
164	planning the coverage work, not previously recorded.
165	
166	The three methods carried the DevDesk context in the `path` field of the git
167	credential protocol (`path=devdesk/context/<name>`). Git discards that field
168	unless `credential.useHttpPath` is set, which is off by default, so every
169	credential was keyed on `protocol://host` alone. Two contexts pointing at the
170	same GitLab host silently overwrote each other, and the last one to authenticate
171	won for all of them. Verified against a real `git credential` store before and
172	after the fix; it affects every helper (GCM, wincred, osxkeychain), since git
173	strips the path before the helper is ever called.
174	
175	**Fix:** pass `-c credential.useHttpPath=true` on each invocation. Scoping it to
176	the call leaves the user's git configuration alone — setting it globally would
177	change credential resolution for every repository on the machine. Pinned by
178	`TestGitCredentialIsolatesContexts`.
179	
180	Existing users must re-authenticate: credentials saved under the old
181	path-stripped key no longer match. Those credentials were ambiguous across
182	contexts anyway.
183	
184	Two smaller defects went with it:
185	
186	- `Delete` had no timeout, while `Save` and `Load` bounded themselves to 2 s
187	  precisely so an unconfigured helper could not freeze the TUI. Logout could
188	  hang indefinitely.
189	- The timeout killed only the direct `git` child, though its comment claimed
190	  otherwise. The helper git spawns survives and holds the output pipes open, so
191	  `Run` kept blocking. All three calls now share one `runCredential` helper built
192	  on `exec.CommandContext` plus `WaitDelay`, which bounds the wait on those pipes.
193	
194	`internal/credentials/helper.go` (`HelperStorage`, 137 lines) was deleted rather
195	than fixed: nothing outside its own tests constructed it. It was also broken —
196	`detectHelper()` returns whatever `git config credential.helper` holds, so a
197	common value like `store --file=/path` became the single unfindable command
198	`credential-store --file=/path` — and it hardcoded `protocol=https`, unlike
199	`GitCredentialStorage`, which reads the scheme from the URL.
200	
201	---
202	
203	## 2. Technical debt
204	
205	### Test coverage
206	
207	Currently **43.6 %** overall; the agreed target is 80 %, which needs roughly
208	**+7 250 covered statements** over today's ~2 100.
209	
210	Phased plan, with the harness and most of phase 1 delivered:
211	
212	| Phase | Scope | Status |
213	|---|---|---|
214	| 0 | `internal/ui/testutil` Bubble Tea harness | **done** (100 %) |
215	| 1 | Leaf components and pure helpers | **done** except the `ui/theme` complement (~55 stmts) |
216	| 2 | Mid-size view state machines (`status`, `containers`, `dashboard`, `gitlab/auth`) | **done** |
217	| 3 | Large views (`workspaces`, `explorer`, `security`, `netdiag`) | **in progress** — `netdiag` and `workspaces` done, two left |
218	| 4 | `ui/oci_resources` | pending (~1 995 stmts) |
219	| 5 | Router and I/O seams (`app`, `scan`, `docker`) | pending (~1 360 stmts) |
220	| 6 | Remainder to reach 80 % | pending (~400 stmts) |
221	
222	Phase 1 progress:
223	
224	| Package | Before | Now |
225	|---|---|---|
226	| `internal/ui/testutil` | — | **100 %** (new) |
227	| `internal/ui/shortcut` | 0 % | **100 %** |
228	| `internal/ui/help` | 0 % | **96.7 %** |
229	| `internal/ui/components` | 0 % | **80.2 %** |
230	| `internal/oci` | 0 % | **37.3 %** |
231	| `internal/docker` | 7.3 % | **65.4 %** (phase 5, pulled forward — see below) |
232	| `internal/gitlab` | 7.5 % | **100 %** |
233	| `internal/credentials` | 29.5 % | **98.2 %** |
234	
235	`internal/oci` stops at 37.3 % because the remaining statements are registry HTTP
236	paths (`DownloadTemplate`, `listCatalog`, `ListTemplates`) that need a fuller
237	`httptest` fixture — a manifest plus a gzipped layer — rather than the
238	single-response stubs used so far.
239	
240	Phase 5's blocker is cleared for `docker`: the package now routes every CLI
241	invocation through the `dockerRunner` seam in `internal/docker/exec.go`, so tests
242	drive argument building and output parsing against canned output. `scan` and
243	`app` remain.
244	
245	`internal/gitlab` needed no seam: every function takes a `*gitlabclient.Client`
246	built from a base URL, so an `httptest` server standing in for the API covers
247	the whole package. `Clone` is exercised against a throwaway local repository
248	rather than mocked, and skips when no `git` binary is on `PATH`.
249	
250	Phase 2, complete:
251	
252	| Package | Before | Now |
253	|---|---|---|
254	| `internal/ui/status` | 0 % | **93.9 %** |
255	| `internal/ui/status/components` | 0 % | **93.2 %** |
256	| `internal/ui/containers` | 0 % | **87.2 %** |
257	| `internal/ui/dashboard` | 0 % | **81.5 %** |
258	| `internal/ui/gitlab/auth` | 0 % | **94.5 %** |
259	
260	The view layer needed no seam either, for the reason `internal/ui/testutil`
261	documents: constructors are pure and `Update()` is a pure function, so feeding
262	synthetic messages fully determines the resulting state. No test executes a
263	command Update returns — they shell out to Docker, hit the GitLab API, sleep for
264	a second or open a browser — so the assertions are on model state instead. The
265	few places that must touch disk (`config.Load` after a save, `config.Save`)
266	redirect `HOME` and `USERPROFILE` at a temporary directory, the same trick
267	`internal/credentials` uses.
268	
269	Three constraints the phase surfaced, worth knowing before phases 3–5:
270	
271	- **Colour has to be forced to test styling.** Under `go test` lipgloss detects
272	  no TTY, falls back to the Ascii profile and strips every escape sequence — so
273	  any assertion about colour passes whatever the code does. `containers` calls
274	  `lipgloss.SetColorProfile(termenv.TrueColor)` for the tests that need it and
275	  restores it afterwards; that is what makes the Rule 122 check (no escape
276	  sequences in `table.Row` cells) real rather than vacuous. Verified by styling
277	  a cell on purpose and watching the test fail. `termenv` moved to a direct
278	  dependency for this.
279	- **`bubbles/table` keeps its styles unexported**, so `refreshSelectionStyle` is
280	  asserted by looking for the error-selection escape sequence in the rendered
281	  table rather than by reading `Styles()`.
282	- **`sort.Slice` is not stable**, so fixtures must give every sortable column a
283	  total order or the expected sequences are ambiguous.
284	
285	Phase 3, in progress:
286	
287	| Package | Before | Now |
288	|---|---|---|
289	| `internal/ui/netdiag` | 15.9 % | **86.1 %** |
290	| `internal/ui/workspaces` | 0 % | **81.3 %** |
291	
292	The three-step order held on both: surface pass 58.8 % / 60.3 %, split with the
293	figure unchanged to the statement, completion pass to 86.1 % / 81.3 %.
294	
295	`workspaces` added one technique worth reusing: its filesystem commands
296	(`createWorkspace`, `deleteEntry`, `renameEntry`, `loadEntries`, `enrichEntry`)
297	are **executed** rather than asserted on identity, against `t.TempDir()` and a
298	throwaway git repository. That is what proves the branch, remote and dirty-tree
299	counters are read correctly; a stub would only prove the stub works. It skips
300	when `git` is not on `PATH`, like `internal/gitlab` does. Only the Docker- and
301	desktop-backed commands are left alone.
302	
303	The rest of phase 3 is `gitlab/explorer` (1402 lines) and `security` (1977).
304	
305	Two handlers are deliberately left uncovered in `containers`: `s` and `S` call
306	`detectShell`, which runs `docker exec` synchronously *inside* `Update`. The
307	tests drive those keys only in states that return before reaching it. The same
308	shape appears in `status.reloadConfigAndCheck`, which calls `config.Load()` from
309	`Update`. Neither is a Rule 110 violation — nothing mutates the model from a
310	`Cmd` — but I/O in `Update` blocks the event loop and is untestable without a
311	seam. Worth a look when phase 5 gets to the router.
312	
313	`internal/credentials` needed no seam either. `git credential` is steerable
314	through the environment, so the tests redirect `HOME`, `GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL` and
315	`GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM` at a temporary directory and run the real binary against a
316	throwaway `store` helper — nothing reaches the developer's keychain. Running the
317	real git is what surfaced the context-isolation defect recorded in §1.1; a stub
318	would have frozen the broken behaviour instead. The 2 s timeout is covered by
319	installing a credential helper that sleeps.
320	
321	### Files over the 800-line ceiling
322	
323	The project's own coding rules cap files at 800 lines. Five still exceed it:
324	
325	| File | Lines |
326	|---|---|
327	| `internal/ui/security/model.go` | 1977 |
328	| `internal/ui/oci_resources/update.go` | 1556 |
329	| `internal/ui/gitlab/explorer/model.go` | 1402 |
330	| `internal/app/app.go` | 1333 |
331	| `internal/ui/oci_resources/registry_browser.go` | 822 |
332	
333	`internal/ui/netdiag/model.go` (1114 lines) was split into `validation.go`,
334	`update.go`, `run.go`, `view.go` and `header.go`; the largest is now 314 lines
335	and `model.go` itself is 172. `topology_model.go` stays at 752 — under the
336	ceiling, and its parsers and renderer belong together.
337	
338	`internal/ui/workspaces/model.go` (1299 lines) was split into `messages.go`,
339	`table.go`, `entry.go`, `actions.go` and `update.go`; the largest is 450 and
340	`model.go` itself is 129. `entry.go` is the one worth noticing: the pure and
341	filesystem-only helpers now sit together instead of at the bottom of a
342	1300-line model, which is what made them straightforward to cover.
343	
344	`internal/docker/client.go` (1176 lines — the 1069 recorded earlier was stale)
345	was split into `exec.go`, `containers.go`, `images.go`, `networks.go`,
346	`volumes.go`, `registry.go`, `launch.go`, `system.go` and `parse.go`; the largest
347	is now 269 lines. The former `network.go` became `ports.go`, since it reports the
348	host's listening sockets via `ss` rather than Docker networks — the name was
349	free for the `docker network` family.
350	
351	This interacts with the coverage work: writing several thousand statements of
352	tests against these files before splitting them freezes their current structure.
353	Decide the order deliberately. Splitting `docker` first was the cheap case — its
354	7.3 % coverage meant almost no tests were pinned to the old shape.
355	
356	**The order settled on for phase 3 is: surface tests, then split, then complete
357	coverage** — per package, so each split has a net under it without the tests
358	being written against a layout that is about to change. It worked on `netdiag`:
359	the surface pass reached 58.8 % driving `Update()` and `View()` only, the split
360	moved five blocks of code with the coverage figure unchanged to the statement,
361	and the completion pass took it to 86.1 %. The discipline that makes it work is
362	asserting on behaviour rather than on internals — no test named a file, and the
363	only ones that reach into the model do so for state the view has no other way to
364	expose.
365	
366	### Race detector cannot run locally
367	
368	`mise run test-race` needs cgo and therefore a C compiler on `PATH`. Without one
369	it fails with `cgo: C compiler "gcc" not found`. Bubble Tea `Cmd`s run
370	concurrently, so this is the check most likely to catch a Rule 110 violation.
371	
372	**Now covered by CI.** `.github/workflows/ci.yml` runs `mise run test-race` on
373	every push and pull request, on `ubuntu-latest`, which has a toolchain. The first
374	run reported no data race across all 17 packages.
375	
376	That is a baseline, not a clean bill of health: the detector only sees code the
377	tests actually execute, and coverage is 43.6 %. Rule 110 violations in untested
378	paths — most of the view layer — remain invisible. The two efforts compound, so
379	this is an argument for the coverage phases rather than a substitute for them.
380	Phase 2 puts the first full view state machine under the detector.
381	
382	Installing a local toolchain is still worth doing for anyone touching `Cmd`s, to
383	avoid learning about a race from CI after the fact.
384	
385	---
386	
387	## 3. Planned features
388	
389	Carried over from `todo.md`.
390	
391	### 3.1 Network diagnostics
392	
393	- **Port-forwarding manager** — an interactive dashboard to manage port
394	  redirections to the host machine.
395	
396	### 3.2 Interactive security remediation
397	
398	- **Auto-patch assistance** — after a Trivy scan, offer to generate a patch or an
399	  updated `Dockerfile` that bumps the base image version to clear critical CVEs.
400	- **Local SAST** — wire security linters (Gitleaks for secrets, IaC linters)
401	  directly into the Workspace view.
402	
403	### 3.3 OCI build and cache analyser
404	
405	- **Layer visualisation** — analyse a local image and show the size of each
406	  layer, in the spirit of `dive`. Intended approach:
407	  - Integrated via `google/go-containerregistry` ("daemonless", no dependency on
408	    the Docker daemon).
409	  - Talk to OCI registries directly, pulling manifests and configs without
410	    downloading the whole image.
411	  - Stream layers in memory (`tar`) to rebuild the filesystem tree.
412	  - Compute wasted space by detecting whiteout files (`.wh.`).
413	- **Cache-miss analysis** — explain why a build's cache was invalidated, e.g.
414	  "`package.json` changed, invalidating the cache".
415	
416	### 3.4 Spontaneous dev containers
417	
418	- **Configuration injection** — inject the developer's dotfiles (vim, zsh,
419	  aliases) when opening a terminal inside a container.
420	- **Hot volume mount** — mount the current working directory into a running
421	  container on the fly, to test a local script without rebuilding the image.
422	
423	### 3.5 Resource dashboard (embedded mini-htop)
424	
425	- **TUI charts** — braille-character charts showing live CPU, RAM and network I/O
426	  for every container in the selected project.
427	- **Visual alerts** — user-defined thresholds (e.g. memory saturation).
428	
429	### 3.6 GitHub support alongside GitLab, one active forge per context
430	
431	Support GitHub as well as GitLab, with **exactly one backend active per
432	configuration context**. A context targets one forge; switching forge means
433	switching context.
434	
435	Not started. The notes below are what the current code imposes on the design,
436	not a chosen design.
437	
438	#### What is coupled to GitLab today
439	
440	| Surface | Size |
441	|---|---|
442	| `internal/gitlab` + `internal/ui/gitlab/{auth,explorer}` | ~3 900 lines |
443	| Direct uses of `*gitlabclient.Client` outside `internal/gitlab` | 66, across 8 files |
444	
445	The concrete SDK type leaks into `internal/shared/state.go:57`
446	(`GitLabClient *gitlabclient.Client`), so every consumer is bound to go-gitlab
447	rather than to a DevDesk abstraction. That field is the load-bearing change: an
448	interface there is what makes a second forge possible at all.
449	
450	Also GitLab-shaped: `GitLabConfig` in `internal/config/config.go:41` (URL, token,
451	clone method, pull settings), the `gitlab-auth` / `gitlab-explorer` view names
452	and their `gla` / `gle` aliases in `internal/command/parser.go`, and
453	`shared.GitLabStats`.
454	
455	#### Model mismatches to settle before coding
456	
457	These are not implementation details; they decide what the abstraction can even
458	promise.
459	
460	- **Nesting.** The explorer is a tree of groups → subgroups → projects. GitHub
461	  has no nested groups: an organisation holds repositories, flat. Either the
462	  tree degrades to two levels for GitHub, or the abstraction exposes a depth the
463	  backend declares.
464	- **Deletion.** `DeleteGroup` / `DeleteProject` implement GitLab's two-step
465	  permanent delete (schedule, then purge under the renamed
466	  `-deletion_scheduled-<id>` path). GitHub deletes immediately and has no
467	  equivalent, so the "permanent" checkbox is meaningless there. The `locked`
468	  flag added in §1.1 is the hook for that: a GitHub backend would set it and
469	  leave the box out of reach, as the already-scheduled GitLab case does.
470	- **Dashboard counters.** `FetchDashboardStats` reads `X-Total` from five list
471	  endpoints. GitHub has no equivalent header for these; the counts come from the
472	  search API (`search/issues?q=is:open+is:pr+assignee:@me`), with different rate
473	  limits and semantics.
474	- **Vocabulary.** Group/project/merge request vs organisation/repository/pull
475	  request. The UI must pick per-backend labels or a neutral vocabulary; Rule 129
476	  applies either way.
477	
478	#### Open decision: Go SDKs or the `gh` / `glab` CLIs
479	
480	Worth deciding before any code is written, because it determines whether the
481	package needs a seam.
482	
483	Arguments for the CLIs:
484	
485	- Authentication is already solved, including OAuth device flow, self-hosted
486	  hosts and token storage. DevDesk's own credential handling could shrink — and
487	  it has already proven fragile (see §1.1).
488	- `gh api` and `glab api` are raw REST/GraphQL passthroughs, so no SDK is needed
489	  for coverage of endpoints the abstraction does not model.
490	- No SDK version churn to track for two forges.
491	
492	Arguments against:
493	
494	- **Per-context isolation conflicts with how these tools store auth.** Both keep
495	  global per-host state (`~/.config/gh/hosts.yml`). DevDesk contexts want
496	  *different tokens for the same host*. Driving `gh auth switch` from the TUI
497	  would mutate the user's global CLI state — the exact mistake avoided in §1.1 by
498	  scoping `credential.useHttpPath` to the invocation. The clean route is
499	  `GH_TOKEN` / `GITLAB_TOKEN` per invocation, but then DevDesk still owns the
500	  tokens and the main benefit is gone.
501	- **Two more hard dependencies.** Today DevDesk needs `git`, and `docker` only
502	  for the features that use it. Requiring `gh` and `glab` for the core forge
503	  feature is a real setup-friction regression.
504	- **Cost per call.** A process spawn per request, against a reused HTTP
505	  connection today. The dashboard alone issues five calls, and the explorer
506	  paginates.
507	- **Testability regresses.** `internal/gitlab` reaches 100 % with no seam,
508	  because the SDK takes a base URL that an `httptest` server can stand in for.
509	  Shelling out would put it back in the position `internal/docker` was in, needing
510	  a manufactured seam — and stubbed CLI output encodes assumptions about the tool
511	  rather than testing against it.
512	
513	**Current recommendation:** keep Go SDKs (go-gitlab, go-github) for the API
514	surface, and use the CLIs only as an *optional* token source — when a context has
515	no token, offer to read one from `gh auth token --hostname <host>` or
516	`glab auth status`. That takes the convenience without the coupling. Recorded as
517	a recommendation, not a decision.
518	
519	#### Sketch of the work
520	
521	1. Define a `forge` abstraction from what the code actually consumes: current
522	   user, namespace tree, create/delete namespace and repository, initial commit,
523	   dashboard counters, clone URL.
524	2. Replace `shared.State.GitLabClient` with that interface. This is the change
525	   the other 65 call sites follow from.
526	3. Generalise `GitLabConfig` into a per-context forge config carrying a
527	   `type: gitlab | github` discriminator, and migrate existing config files.
528	4. Implement the GitLab backend by moving the existing code behind the
529	   interface — behaviour-preserving, and covered by the tests added in #7.
530	5. Implement the GitHub backend.
531	6. Rename the views and commands, keeping `gla` / `gle` as aliases so muscle
532	   memory survives.
533	
534	Steps 1–4 are worth doing on their own: they are a refactor of working code with
535	tests already in place, and they are what makes step 5 tractable.
536	
537	---
538	
539	## 4. Existing plans
540	
541	Detailed plans live in `.claude/plans/`. One is referenced directly from the old
542	`todo.md` and is still outstanding:
543	
544	- [`platform_compatibility_improvements.md`](../.claude/plans/platform_compatibility_improvements.md)
545	  — Docker-layer platform portability.
546

# DevDesk Backlog

**Last Updated:** 2026-08-02

Open work for DevDesk: known defects, technical debt, and planned features.
Replaces the former `todo.md` at the repository root. Items completed there
(network topology visualisation, inter-container ping/curl) have been dropped
rather than carried over.

---

## 1. Known defects

D1, D3 and D6 (the byte-vs-rune lot), then D2, D5 and D7, were fixed; see
[§1.1](#11-fixed). **D4 is the only one left**, and it is waiting on a decision
rather than on work.

### D4 — `DeleteConfirmModal` uses `Tab` for field navigation

`internal/ui/components/delete_confirm_modal.go:89-97`

`tab` / `shift+tab` cycle checkbox → Yes → No. Rule 135 reserves those keys for
tab switching and assigns field navigation to `↑ / ↓` exclusively.

Cosmetic in isolation, but it is the kind of inconsistency Rule 135 exists to
prevent. Changing it alters muscle memory, so it needs a deliberate call rather
than a drive-by fix.

Note that the surrounding code moved when D2 was fixed: `tab` / `shift+tab` now
cycle through `cycleFocus()`, which skips the locked checkbox. Switching to
`↑ / ↓` remains a one-line change to the key names.

### D8 — Write-only CRUD flags and an unreachable handler in the status view

`internal/ui/status/model.go:64-67` and `internal/ui/status/update.go:57-60`

`Model.creating`, `Model.editing` and `Model.confirming` are assigned in five
places and read in none: the view keys off `componentForm != nil` and
`confirmModal != nil` instead. `HasActiveForm`, the one method that read them, is
commented out at `model.go:139`.

`ComponentFormCancelledMsg` is never sent either. `ComponentForm.handleKeyMsg`
answers `esc` by returning a nil form, and the caller stores that — so the
`case components.ComponentFormCancelledMsg` branch in `Update()` cannot run. Its
body is the only thing that would reset `creating` / `editing`, which is why they
would stay true after a cancellation if anything did read them.

Harmless today, but it is state that lies: a reader reasonably assumes those
flags mean something. Found while writing the phase 2 tests; the tests
deliberately assert on `componentForm` / `confirmModal` rather than on the flags,
so removing them breaks nothing.

**Fix:** delete the three fields, the unreachable case and the message type — or
give `esc` a message and make the flags load-bearing. Deleting is the smaller
change and matches how the view already works.

### D9 — The containers list opens sorted Z→A

`internal/ui/containers/model.go:140-147`

`New()` sets neither `sortColumn` nor `sortAsc`, so both take their zero value:
name, *descending*. The status view, which has the same cycle-sort mechanism,
sets `sortAsc: true` explicitly. The header does show `Name ▼`, so the view is
at least honest about it — but nobody chose it, and it disagrees with the other
list view in the application.

**Fix:** set `sortAsc: true` in `New()`, one line. Left for a deliberate call
because it changes what the user sees on open.
`TestDefaultSortIsNameDescending` pins the current behaviour and says so.

### 1.1 Fixed

**Two views' help advertised keys that do nothing.** Found while writing the
phase 2 tests, not previously recorded.

The status view's `GetHelpContent` documented `n` for "Add a new monitor" while
the binding has been `ctrl+n` since Rule 111 standardised it, and the `/` filter
was missing altogether; the empty-state message told the user to "Press [n]" too.
The containers view advertised `S` (shell in a new window) in `GetShortcuts()`
without documenting it at all.

The workspaces view had it too, found in phase 3: `n` and `Enter` documented
where the bindings are `ctrl+n` and `enter`, `/` undocumented, and the same
stale "Press [n]" in its empty state.

All three are fixed, and each package now asserts that every key
`GetShortcuts()` advertises appears in `GetHelpContent()` — the check that would
have caught the drift when it was introduced. Three views in a row carried it,
so assume `explorer` and `security` do as well.

**A stranded cursor in the workspaces table.** `bubbles/table.SetRows` does not
clamp the cursor when the row count shrinks. Drilling into a directory with
fewer entries — or narrowing the filter — left the cursor past the end: nothing
highlighted, and `enter`, `ctrl+d`, `r` and `ctrl+s` all silently did nothing
until the user pressed an arrow key. `updateTableData` now clamps.

The containers view avoids this by calling `GotoTop()` after every filter
change; workspaces had no equivalent. Worth checking in `explorer`, which has
the same drill-down shape.

**D7** (`extractTarGz` kept parent references in archive paths), **D2** (the
"permanent delete" checkbox was documented as locked but was not) and **D5** (an
unreachable focus clamp in `CreationForm`) were fixed together — three small,
independent defects with no shared code.

`extractTarGz` now routes every member name through `sanitizeArchivePath`, which
normalises the separators and rejects anything resolving outside the root.
Cleaning happens *after* the leading separator is stripped, not before:
`path.Clean("/../x")` returns `"/x"`, which would have absorbed the traversal
silently instead of exposing it. Traversal that resolves back inside the root
(`templates/../README.md`) is kept, normalised. Backslashes are folded to `/`
first, so `..\..\etc\passwd` cannot pass as an ordinary filename on a tar reader
that treats it as one.

The delete modal carries a `locked` flag, set only by
`NewDeleteConfirmModalPermanent`. Rather than merely making the toggle a no-op,
navigation skips the checkbox entirely (`minFocus()` / `cycleFocus()`) and the
line renders dimmed: a focusable control that ignores every key is more
confusing than one that is plainly not there.

The `CreationForm` clamp was deleted and replaced by a comment recording why it
cannot fire, so it is not reintroduced defensively. A test pins the invariant it
was guarding.

Both self-annulling tests became real assertions:
`TestDeleteConfirmModalPermanentCheckboxIsStillToggleable` →
`TestDeleteConfirmModalPermanentCheckboxIsLocked` (plus navigation and
confirmation cases), and `TestExtractTarGzPreservesParentTraversalInKeys` →
`TestExtractTarGzRejectsParentTraversal` (table-driven over five escape shapes)
alongside `TestExtractTarGzNormalisesContainedTraversal`.

**D1** (`ReportModal.View()` emitted invalid UTF-8), **D3** (`wrapInputLines`
looped forever when `wrapWidth <= 0`) and **D6** (`wordWrap` measured bytes) were
fixed together, since D1 and D6 were the same byte-vs-rune defect.

Rather than patch each call site, the truncation logic moved into
`internal/ui/theme/text.go` per Rule 117: `StringWidth`, `TruncateWidth` (keeps
the head) and `TruncateTailWidth` (keeps the tail, for paths). All three measure
terminal columns, so double-width glyphs are handled too, not just multibyte
ones.

A **fourth site carried the same defect** and was not recorded here: `truncate`
in `internal/ui/security/model.go` sliced bytes exactly like D1 and rendered
Trivy finding titles. It is now `theme.TruncateWidth` and the local helper is
gone.

A **fifth site** turned up later, during the phase 3 tests: `firstOutputLine` in
`internal/ui/netdiag` sliced `line[:maxLen-3]` to fill the Output column of the
results table, so any diagnostic whose first line contained a multibyte rune
could be cut in half and bleed across the rows below (Rule 122). Now
`theme.TruncateWidth`, pinned by `TestFirstOutputLineKeepsMultibyteRunesIntact`.
Worth grepping for `[:` on strings when the remaining phases land.

The two pinned tests that `t.Skip()`d became real assertions
(`TestReportModalViewKeepsMultibyteRunesIntact`,
`TestWordWrapMeasuresColumnsNotBytes`).

One call site was deliberately left alone: `truncateResultLine` in
`internal/ui/oci_resources/connectivity_form.go` counts runes rather than bytes,
so it is correct — merely imprecise on double-width glyphs. Folding it into the
theme helpers is a cleanup, not a defect fix.

**Context isolation in `GitCredentialStorage` never worked.** Found while
planning the coverage work, not previously recorded.

The three methods carried the DevDesk context in the `path` field of the git
credential protocol (`path=devdesk/context/<name>`). Git discards that field
unless `credential.useHttpPath` is set, which is off by default, so every
credential was keyed on `protocol://host` alone. Two contexts pointing at the
same GitLab host silently overwrote each other, and the last one to authenticate
won for all of them. Verified against a real `git credential` store before and
after the fix; it affects every helper (GCM, wincred, osxkeychain), since git
strips the path before the helper is ever called.

**Fix:** pass `-c credential.useHttpPath=true` on each invocation. Scoping it to
the call leaves the user's git configuration alone — setting it globally would
change credential resolution for every repository on the machine. Pinned by
`TestGitCredentialIsolatesContexts`.

Existing users must re-authenticate: credentials saved under the old
path-stripped key no longer match. Those credentials were ambiguous across
contexts anyway.

Two smaller defects went with it:

- `Delete` had no timeout, while `Save` and `Load` bounded themselves to 2 s
  precisely so an unconfigured helper could not freeze the TUI. Logout could
  hang indefinitely.
- The timeout killed only the direct `git` child, though its comment claimed
  otherwise. The helper git spawns survives and holds the output pipes open, so
  `Run` kept blocking. All three calls now share one `runCredential` helper built
  on `exec.CommandContext` plus `WaitDelay`, which bounds the wait on those pipes.

`internal/credentials/helper.go` (`HelperStorage`, 137 lines) was deleted rather
than fixed: nothing outside its own tests constructed it. It was also broken —
`detectHelper()` returns whatever `git config credential.helper` holds, so a
common value like `store --file=/path` became the single unfindable command
`credential-store --file=/path` — and it hardcoded `protocol=https`, unlike
`GitCredentialStorage`, which reads the scheme from the URL.

---

## 2. Technical debt

### Test coverage

Currently **43.6 %** overall; the agreed target is 80 %, which needs roughly
**+7 250 covered statements** over today's ~2 100.

Phased plan, with the harness and most of phase 1 delivered:

| Phase | Scope | Status |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | `internal/ui/testutil` Bubble Tea harness | **done** (100 %) |
| 1 | Leaf components and pure helpers | **done** except the `ui/theme` complement (~55 stmts) |
| 2 | Mid-size view state machines (`status`, `containers`, `dashboard`, `gitlab/auth`) | **done** |
| 3 | Large views (`workspaces`, `explorer`, `security`, `netdiag`) | **in progress** — `netdiag` and `workspaces` done, two left |
| 4 | `ui/oci_resources` | pending (~1 995 stmts) |
| 5 | Router and I/O seams (`app`, `scan`, `docker`) | pending (~1 360 stmts) |
| 6 | Remainder to reach 80 % | pending (~400 stmts) |

Phase 1 progress:

| Package | Before | Now |
|---|---|---|
| `internal/ui/testutil` | — | **100 %** (new) |
| `internal/ui/shortcut` | 0 % | **100 %** |
| `internal/ui/help` | 0 % | **96.7 %** |
| `internal/ui/components` | 0 % | **80.2 %** |
| `internal/oci` | 0 % | **37.3 %** |
| `internal/docker` | 7.3 % | **65.4 %** (phase 5, pulled forward — see below) |
| `internal/gitlab` | 7.5 % | **100 %** |
| `internal/credentials` | 29.5 % | **98.2 %** |

`internal/oci` stops at 37.3 % because the remaining statements are registry HTTP
paths (`DownloadTemplate`, `listCatalog`, `ListTemplates`) that need a fuller
`httptest` fixture — a manifest plus a gzipped layer — rather than the
single-response stubs used so far.

Phase 5's blocker is cleared for `docker`: the package now routes every CLI
invocation through the `dockerRunner` seam in `internal/docker/exec.go`, so tests
drive argument building and output parsing against canned output. `scan` and
`app` remain.

`internal/gitlab` needed no seam: every function takes a `*gitlabclient.Client`
built from a base URL, so an `httptest` server standing in for the API covers
the whole package. `Clone` is exercised against a throwaway local repository
rather than mocked, and skips when no `git` binary is on `PATH`.

Phase 2, complete:

| Package | Before | Now |
|---|---|---|
| `internal/ui/status` | 0 % | **93.9 %** |
| `internal/ui/status/components` | 0 % | **93.2 %** |
| `internal/ui/containers` | 0 % | **87.2 %** |
| `internal/ui/dashboard` | 0 % | **81.5 %** |
| `internal/ui/gitlab/auth` | 0 % | **94.5 %** |

The view layer needed no seam either, for the reason `internal/ui/testutil`
documents: constructors are pure and `Update()` is a pure function, so feeding
synthetic messages fully determines the resulting state. No test executes a
command Update returns — they shell out to Docker, hit the GitLab API, sleep for
a second or open a browser — so the assertions are on model state instead. The
few places that must touch disk (`config.Load` after a save, `config.Save`)
redirect `HOME` and `USERPROFILE` at a temporary directory, the same trick
`internal/credentials` uses.

Three constraints the phase surfaced, worth knowing before phases 3–5:

- **Colour has to be forced to test styling.** Under `go test` lipgloss detects
  no TTY, falls back to the Ascii profile and strips every escape sequence — so
  any assertion about colour passes whatever the code does. `containers` calls
  `lipgloss.SetColorProfile(termenv.TrueColor)` for the tests that need it and
  restores it afterwards; that is what makes the Rule 122 check (no escape
  sequences in `table.Row` cells) real rather than vacuous. Verified by styling
  a cell on purpose and watching the test fail. `termenv` moved to a direct
  dependency for this.
- **`bubbles/table` keeps its styles unexported**, so `refreshSelectionStyle` is
  asserted by looking for the error-selection escape sequence in the rendered
  table rather than by reading `Styles()`.
- **`sort.Slice` is not stable**, so fixtures must give every sortable column a
  total order or the expected sequences are ambiguous.

Phase 3, in progress:

| Package | Before | Now |
|---|---|---|
| `internal/ui/netdiag` | 15.9 % | **86.1 %** |
| `internal/ui/workspaces` | 0 % | **81.3 %** |

The three-step order held on both: surface pass 58.8 % / 60.3 %, split with the
figure unchanged to the statement, completion pass to 86.1 % / 81.3 %.

`workspaces` added one technique worth reusing: its filesystem commands
(`createWorkspace`, `deleteEntry`, `renameEntry`, `loadEntries`, `enrichEntry`)
are **executed** rather than asserted on identity, against `t.TempDir()` and a
throwaway git repository. That is what proves the branch, remote and dirty-tree
counters are read correctly; a stub would only prove the stub works. It skips
when `git` is not on `PATH`, like `internal/gitlab` does. Only the Docker- and
desktop-backed commands are left alone.

The rest of phase 3 is `gitlab/explorer` (1402 lines) and `security` (1977).

Two handlers are deliberately left uncovered in `containers`: `s` and `S` call
`detectShell`, which runs `docker exec` synchronously *inside* `Update`. The
tests drive those keys only in states that return before reaching it. The same
shape appears in `status.reloadConfigAndCheck`, which calls `config.Load()` from
`Update`. Neither is a Rule 110 violation — nothing mutates the model from a
`Cmd` — but I/O in `Update` blocks the event loop and is untestable without a
seam. Worth a look when phase 5 gets to the router.

`internal/credentials` needed no seam either. `git credential` is steerable
through the environment, so the tests redirect `HOME`, `GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL` and
`GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM` at a temporary directory and run the real binary against a
throwaway `store` helper — nothing reaches the developer's keychain. Running the
real git is what surfaced the context-isolation defect recorded in §1.1; a stub
would have frozen the broken behaviour instead. The 2 s timeout is covered by
installing a credential helper that sleeps.

### Files over the 800-line ceiling

The project's own coding rules cap files at 800 lines. Five still exceed it:

| File | Lines |
|---|---|
| `internal/ui/security/model.go` | 1977 |
| `internal/ui/oci_resources/update.go` | 1556 |
| `internal/ui/gitlab/explorer/model.go` | 1402 |
| `internal/app/app.go` | 1333 |
| `internal/ui/oci_resources/registry_browser.go` | 822 |

`internal/ui/netdiag/model.go` (1114 lines) was split into `validation.go`,
`update.go`, `run.go`, `view.go` and `header.go`; the largest is now 314 lines
and `model.go` itself is 172. `topology_model.go` stays at 752 — under the
ceiling, and its parsers and renderer belong together.

`internal/ui/workspaces/model.go` (1299 lines) was split into `messages.go`,
`table.go`, `entry.go`, `actions.go` and `update.go`; the largest is 450 and
`model.go` itself is 129. `entry.go` is the one worth noticing: the pure and
filesystem-only helpers now sit together instead of at the bottom of a
1300-line model, which is what made them straightforward to cover.

`internal/docker/client.go` (1176 lines — the 1069 recorded earlier was stale)
was split into `exec.go`, `containers.go`, `images.go`, `networks.go`,
`volumes.go`, `registry.go`, `launch.go`, `system.go` and `parse.go`; the largest
is now 269 lines. The former `network.go` became `ports.go`, since it reports the
host's listening sockets via `ss` rather than Docker networks — the name was
free for the `docker network` family.

This interacts with the coverage work: writing several thousand statements of
tests against these files before splitting them freezes their current structure.
Decide the order deliberately. Splitting `docker` first was the cheap case — its
7.3 % coverage meant almost no tests were pinned to the old shape.

**The order settled on for phase 3 is: surface tests, then split, then complete
coverage** — per package, so each split has a net under it without the tests
being written against a layout that is about to change. It worked on `netdiag`:
the surface pass reached 58.8 % driving `Update()` and `View()` only, the split
moved five blocks of code with the coverage figure unchanged to the statement,
and the completion pass took it to 86.1 %. The discipline that makes it work is
asserting on behaviour rather than on internals — no test named a file, and the
only ones that reach into the model do so for state the view has no other way to
expose.

### Race detector cannot run locally

`mise run test-race` needs cgo and therefore a C compiler on `PATH`. Without one
it fails with `cgo: C compiler "gcc" not found`. Bubble Tea `Cmd`s run
concurrently, so this is the check most likely to catch a Rule 110 violation.

**Now covered by CI.** `.github/workflows/ci.yml` runs `mise run test-race` on
every push and pull request, on `ubuntu-latest`, which has a toolchain. The first
run reported no data race across all 17 packages.

That is a baseline, not a clean bill of health: the detector only sees code the
tests actually execute, and coverage is 43.6 %. Rule 110 violations in untested
paths — most of the view layer — remain invisible. The two efforts compound, so
this is an argument for the coverage phases rather than a substitute for them.
Phase 2 puts the first full view state machine under the detector.

Installing a local toolchain is still worth doing for anyone touching `Cmd`s, to
avoid learning about a race from CI after the fact.

---

## 3. Planned features

Carried over from `todo.md`.

### 3.1 Network diagnostics

- **Port-forwarding manager** — an interactive dashboard to manage port
  redirections to the host machine.

### 3.2 Interactive security remediation

- **Auto-patch assistance** — after a Trivy scan, offer to generate a patch or an
  updated `Dockerfile` that bumps the base image version to clear critical CVEs.
- **Local SAST** — wire security linters (Gitleaks for secrets, IaC linters)
  directly into the Workspace view.

### 3.3 OCI build and cache analyser

- **Layer visualisation** — analyse a local image and show the size of each
  layer, in the spirit of `dive`. Intended approach:
  - Integrated via `google/go-containerregistry` ("daemonless", no dependency on
    the Docker daemon).
  - Talk to OCI registries directly, pulling manifests and configs without
    downloading the whole image.
  - Stream layers in memory (`tar`) to rebuild the filesystem tree.
  - Compute wasted space by detecting whiteout files (`.wh.`).
- **Cache-miss analysis** — explain why a build's cache was invalidated, e.g.
  "`package.json` changed, invalidating the cache".

### 3.4 Spontaneous dev containers

- **Configuration injection** — inject the developer's dotfiles (vim, zsh,
  aliases) when opening a terminal inside a container.
- **Hot volume mount** — mount the current working directory into a running
  container on the fly, to test a local script without rebuilding the image.

### 3.5 Resource dashboard (embedded mini-htop)

- **TUI charts** — braille-character charts showing live CPU, RAM and network I/O
  for every container in the selected project.
- **Visual alerts** — user-defined thresholds (e.g. memory saturation).

### 3.6 GitHub support alongside GitLab, one active forge per context

Support GitHub as well as GitLab, with **exactly one backend active per
configuration context**. A context targets one forge; switching forge means
switching context.

Not started. The notes below are what the current code imposes on the design,
not a chosen design.

#### What is coupled to GitLab today

| Surface | Size |
|---|---|
| `internal/gitlab` + `internal/ui/gitlab/{auth,explorer}` | ~3 900 lines |
| Direct uses of `*gitlabclient.Client` outside `internal/gitlab` | 66, across 8 files |

The concrete SDK type leaks into `internal/shared/state.go:57`
(`GitLabClient *gitlabclient.Client`), so every consumer is bound to go-gitlab
rather than to a DevDesk abstraction. That field is the load-bearing change: an
interface there is what makes a second forge possible at all.

Also GitLab-shaped: `GitLabConfig` in `internal/config/config.go:41` (URL, token,
clone method, pull settings), the `gitlab-auth` / `gitlab-explorer` view names
and their `gla` / `gle` aliases in `internal/command/parser.go`, and
`shared.GitLabStats`.

#### Model mismatches to settle before coding

These are not implementation details; they decide what the abstraction can even
promise.

- **Nesting.** The explorer is a tree of groups → subgroups → projects. GitHub
  has no nested groups: an organisation holds repositories, flat. Either the
  tree degrades to two levels for GitHub, or the abstraction exposes a depth the
  backend declares.
- **Deletion.** `DeleteGroup` / `DeleteProject` implement GitLab's two-step
  permanent delete (schedule, then purge under the renamed
  `-deletion_scheduled-<id>` path). GitHub deletes immediately and has no
  equivalent, so the "permanent" checkbox is meaningless there. The `locked`
  flag added in §1.1 is the hook for that: a GitHub backend would set it and
  leave the box out of reach, as the already-scheduled GitLab case does.
- **Dashboard counters.** `FetchDashboardStats` reads `X-Total` from five list
  endpoints. GitHub has no equivalent header for these; the counts come from the
  search API (`search/issues?q=is:open+is:pr+assignee:@me`), with different rate
  limits and semantics.
- **Vocabulary.** Group/project/merge request vs organisation/repository/pull
  request. The UI must pick per-backend labels or a neutral vocabulary; Rule 129
  applies either way.

#### Open decision: Go SDKs or the `gh` / `glab` CLIs

Worth deciding before any code is written, because it determines whether the
package needs a seam.

Arguments for the CLIs:

- Authentication is already solved, including OAuth device flow, self-hosted
  hosts and token storage. DevDesk's own credential handling could shrink — and
  it has already proven fragile (see §1.1).
- `gh api` and `glab api` are raw REST/GraphQL passthroughs, so no SDK is needed
  for coverage of endpoints the abstraction does not model.
- No SDK version churn to track for two forges.

Arguments against:

- **Per-context isolation conflicts with how these tools store auth.** Both keep
  global per-host state (`~/.config/gh/hosts.yml`). DevDesk contexts want
  *different tokens for the same host*. Driving `gh auth switch` from the TUI
  would mutate the user's global CLI state — the exact mistake avoided in §1.1 by
  scoping `credential.useHttpPath` to the invocation. The clean route is
  `GH_TOKEN` / `GITLAB_TOKEN` per invocation, but then DevDesk still owns the
  tokens and the main benefit is gone.
- **Two more hard dependencies.** Today DevDesk needs `git`, and `docker` only
  for the features that use it. Requiring `gh` and `glab` for the core forge
  feature is a real setup-friction regression.
- **Cost per call.** A process spawn per request, against a reused HTTP
  connection today. The dashboard alone issues five calls, and the explorer
  paginates.
- **Testability regresses.** `internal/gitlab` reaches 100 % with no seam,
  because the SDK takes a base URL that an `httptest` server can stand in for.
  Shelling out would put it back in the position `internal/docker` was in, needing
  a manufactured seam — and stubbed CLI output encodes assumptions about the tool
  rather than testing against it.

**Current recommendation:** keep Go SDKs (go-gitlab, go-github) for the API
surface, and use the CLIs only as an *optional* token source — when a context has
no token, offer to read one from `gh auth token --hostname <host>` or
`glab auth status`. That takes the convenience without the coupling. Recorded as
a recommendation, not a decision.

#### Sketch of the work

1. Define a `forge` abstraction from what the code actually consumes: current
   user, namespace tree, create/delete namespace and repository, initial commit,
   dashboard counters, clone URL.
2. Replace `shared.State.GitLabClient` with that interface. This is the change
   the other 65 call sites follow from.
3. Generalise `GitLabConfig` into a per-context forge config carrying a
   `type: gitlab | github` discriminator, and migrate existing config files.
4. Implement the GitLab backend by moving the existing code behind the
   interface — behaviour-preserving, and covered by the tests added in #7.
5. Implement the GitHub backend.
6. Rename the views and commands, keeping `gla` / `gle` as aliases so muscle
   memory survives.

Steps 1–4 are worth doing on their own: they are a refactor of working code with
tests already in place, and they are what makes step 5 tractable.

Steps 1–4 are worth doing on their own: they are a refactor of working code with
tests already in place, and they are what makes step 5 tractable.

### 3.7 A command-mode key that works from inside a text field

Requested: enter command mode with a modifier chord rather than a bare `:`,
because the application is full of text inputs and inside one a `:` does nothing
but insert a colon.

The complaint is accurate and the current design concedes it. `internal/app/app.go:466`
routes `:` through `maybeEnterInCommandMode`, which asks the view whether it is
in edit mode (`FormView.InEditMode()`) and, if it is, forwards the keystroke to
the active input instead. So command mode is unreachable from any form, filter
box or search field — which is most of the application.

An escape hatch already exists and shows the shape of the problem: the
`CommandModeView` interface (`app.go:44`) lets a view declare that `:` should
enter command mode even while `InEditMode()` is true. Exactly one view
implements it — `internal/ui/netdiag/update.go:18` — and only for the topology
tab in its ready state, where nothing is being edited anyway. It papers over a
routing quirk; it does not give the user a way in while typing.

#### `ctrl+:` specifically cannot be made to work

Worth settling before any code is written. A terminal encodes Ctrl by clearing
bits, which only covers ASCII `@` through `_` (0x40–0x5F) plus a handful of
aliases. `:` is 0x3A and has no control encoding: pressing Ctrl+: sends either a
plain `:` or nothing at all. Reporting it as a distinct key needs the Kitty
keyboard protocol or xterm's `modifyOtherKeys`, and bubbletea v1.3.10 implements
neither — the module has no reference to either. A `case "ctrl+:"` would be dead
code.

#### What does work

| Option | Portability | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `alt+:` | Good | bubbletea v1 reports `alt+<rune>` from the ESC-prefix convention; works wherever "Alt sends Escape" is on, which is the default nearly everywhere. Closest to the request. |
| A free `ctrl+<letter>` | Total | The bindings in use are `ctrl+a c d e f k n o r s w y`; `ctrl+i m j h [` are aliases of Tab, Enter, LF, Backspace and Esc and must be left alone. That leaves `b g l p t u v x z` — `ctrl+p` and `ctrl+g` read best. |
| `esc` then `:` | Total | Vim-like, but `esc` already means cancel / go back everywhere (Rule 111), so it would need a mode timer. Not recommended. |

**Recommendation: keep `:` and add one chord that always wins**, rather than
replacing `:`. Muscle memory survives, and the new binding needs no
`InEditMode()` check at all — `handleKeyMsg` sees every `tea.KeyMsg` before any
view does, so a `case` there takes priority unconditionally. That is the whole
implementation: three lines next to the existing `case ":"`.

#### Ripple

- `internal/app/app_header.go:56` renders `:` as the inactive command prompt —
  it should show whichever key is authoritative.
- `internal/app/app_test.go:30` asserts the `:` shortcut.
- Rules 114, 130 and 137: every view's `GetShortcuts()` / `GetHelpContent()` that
  mentions `:`. Three views were already caught drifting on this kind of change
  (§1.1), so the check that each advertised key appears in the help — now present
  in `status`, `containers` and `workspaces` — is the thing to lean on.
- `CommandModeView` / `AllowCommandMode` become deletable if the new chord always
  wins, since the sole reason they exist disappears. One implementation to
  remove.

1	# DevDesk Backlog
2	
3	**Last Updated:** 2026-08-02
4	
5	Open work for DevDesk: known defects, technical debt, and planned features.
6	Replaces the former `todo.md` at the repository root. Items completed there
7	(network topology visualisation, inter-container ping/curl) have been dropped
8	rather than carried over.
9	
10	---
11	
12	## 1. Known defects
13	
14	D1, D3 and D6 (the byte-vs-rune lot), then D2, D5 and D7, were fixed; see
15	[§1.1](#11-fixed). **D4 is the only one left**, and it is waiting on a decision
16	rather than on work.
17	
18	### D4 — `DeleteConfirmModal` uses `Tab` for field navigation
19	
20	`internal/ui/components/delete_confirm_modal.go:89-97`
21	
22	`tab` / `shift+tab` cycle checkbox → Yes → No. Rule 135 reserves those keys for
23	tab switching and assigns field navigation to `↑ / ↓` exclusively.
24	
25	Cosmetic in isolation, but it is the kind of inconsistency Rule 135 exists to
26	prevent. Changing it alters muscle memory, so it needs a deliberate call rather
27	than a drive-by fix.
28	
29	Note that the surrounding code moved when D2 was fixed: `tab` / `shift+tab` now
30	cycle through `cycleFocus()`, which skips the locked checkbox. Switching to
31	`↑ / ↓` remains a one-line change to the key names.
32	
33	### D8 — Write-only CRUD flags and an unreachable handler in the status view
34	
35	`internal/ui/status/model.go:64-67` and `internal/ui/status/update.go:57-60`
36	
37	`Model.creating`, `Model.editing` and `Model.confirming` are assigned in five
38	places and read in none: the view keys off `componentForm != nil` and
39	`confirmModal != nil` instead. `HasActiveForm`, the one method that read them, is
40	commented out at `model.go:139`.
41	
42	`ComponentFormCancelledMsg` is never sent either. `ComponentForm.handleKeyMsg`
43	answers `esc` by returning a nil form, and the caller stores that — so the
44	`case components.ComponentFormCancelledMsg` branch in `Update()` cannot run. Its
45	body is the only thing that would reset `creating` / `editing`, which is why they
46	would stay true after a cancellation if anything did read them.
47	
48	Harmless today, but it is state that lies: a reader reasonably assumes those
49	flags mean something. Found while writing the phase 2 tests; the tests
50	deliberately assert on `componentForm` / `confirmModal` rather than on the flags,
51	so removing them breaks nothing.
52	
53	**Fix:** delete the three fields, the unreachable case and the message type — or
54	give `esc` a message and make the flags load-bearing. Deleting is the smaller
55	change and matches how the view already works.
56	
57	### D9 — The containers list opens sorted Z→A
58	
59	`internal/ui/containers/model.go:140-147`
60	
61	`New()` sets neither `sortColumn` nor `sortAsc`, so both take their zero value:
62	name, *descending*. The status view, which has the same cycle-sort mechanism,
63	sets `sortAsc: true` explicitly. The header does show `Name ▼`, so the view is
64	at least honest about it — but nobody chose it, and it disagrees with the other
65	list view in the application.
66	
67	**Fix:** set `sortAsc: true` in `New()`, one line. Left for a deliberate call
68	because it changes what the user sees on open.
69	`TestDefaultSortIsNameDescending` pins the current behaviour and says so.
70	
71	### 1.1 Fixed
72	
73	**Two views' help advertised keys that do nothing.** Found while writing the
74	phase 2 tests, not previously recorded.
75	
76	The status view's `GetHelpContent` documented `n` for "Add a new monitor" while
77	the binding has been `ctrl+n` since Rule 111 standardised it, and the `/` filter
78	was missing altogether; the empty-state message told the user to "Press [n]" too.
79	The containers view advertised `S` (shell in a new window) in `GetShortcuts()`
80	without documenting it at all.
81	
82	The workspaces view had it too, found in phase 3: `n` and `Enter` documented
83	where the bindings are `ctrl+n` and `enter`, `/` undocumented, and the same
84	stale "Press [n]" in its empty state.
85	
86	All three are fixed, and each package now asserts that every key
87	`GetShortcuts()` advertises appears in `GetHelpContent()` — the check that would
88	have caught the drift when it was introduced. Three views in a row carried it,
89	so assume `explorer` and `security` do as well.
90	
91	**A stranded cursor in the workspaces table.** `bubbles/table.SetRows` does not
92	clamp the cursor when the row count shrinks. Drilling into a directory with
93	fewer entries — or narrowing the filter — left the cursor past the end: nothing
94	highlighted, and `enter`, `ctrl+d`, `r` and `ctrl+s` all silently did nothing
95	until the user pressed an arrow key. `updateTableData` now clamps.
96	
97	The containers view avoids this by calling `GotoTop()` after every filter
98	change; workspaces had no equivalent. Worth checking in `explorer`, which has
99	the same drill-down shape.
100	
101	**D7** (`extractTarGz` kept parent references in archive paths), **D2** (the
102	"permanent delete" checkbox was documented as locked but was not) and **D5** (an
103	unreachable focus clamp in `CreationForm`) were fixed together — three small,
104	independent defects with no shared code.
105	
106	`extractTarGz` now routes every member name through `sanitizeArchivePath`, which
107	normalises the separators and rejects anything resolving outside the root.
108	Cleaning happens *after* the leading separator is stripped, not before:
109	`path.Clean("/../x")` returns `"/x"`, which would have absorbed the traversal
110	silently instead of exposing it. Traversal that resolves back inside the root
111	(`templates/../README.md`) is kept, normalised. Backslashes are folded to `/`
112	first, so `..\..\etc\passwd` cannot pass as an ordinary filename on a tar reader
113	that treats it as one.
114	
115	The delete modal carries a `locked` flag, set only by
116	`NewDeleteConfirmModalPermanent`. Rather than merely making the toggle a no-op,
117	navigation skips the checkbox entirely (`minFocus()` / `cycleFocus()`) and the
118	line renders dimmed: a focusable control that ignores every key is more
119	confusing than one that is plainly not there.
120	
121	The `CreationForm` clamp was deleted and replaced by a comment recording why it
122	cannot fire, so it is not reintroduced defensively. A test pins the invariant it
123	was guarding.
124	
125	Both self-annulling tests became real assertions:
126	`TestDeleteConfirmModalPermanentCheckboxIsStillToggleable` →
127	`TestDeleteConfirmModalPermanentCheckboxIsLocked` (plus navigation and
128	confirmation cases), and `TestExtractTarGzPreservesParentTraversalInKeys` →
129	`TestExtractTarGzRejectsParentTraversal` (table-driven over five escape shapes)
130	alongside `TestExtractTarGzNormalisesContainedTraversal`.
131	
132	**D1** (`ReportModal.View()` emitted invalid UTF-8), **D3** (`wrapInputLines`
133	looped forever when `wrapWidth <= 0`) and **D6** (`wordWrap` measured bytes) were
134	fixed together, since D1 and D6 were the same byte-vs-rune defect.
135	
136	Rather than patch each call site, the truncation logic moved into
137	`internal/ui/theme/text.go` per Rule 117: `StringWidth`, `TruncateWidth` (keeps
138	the head) and `TruncateTailWidth` (keeps the tail, for paths). All three measure
139	terminal columns, so double-width glyphs are handled too, not just multibyte
140	ones.
141	
142	A **fourth site carried the same defect** and was not recorded here: `truncate`
143	in `internal/ui/security/model.go` sliced bytes exactly like D1 and rendered
144	Trivy finding titles. It is now `theme.TruncateWidth` and the local helper is
145	gone.
146	
147	A **fifth site** turned up later, during the phase 3 tests: `firstOutputLine` in
148	`internal/ui/netdiag` sliced `line[:maxLen-3]` to fill the Output column of the
149	results table, so any diagnostic whose first line contained a multibyte rune
150	could be cut in half and bleed across the rows below (Rule 122). Now
151	`theme.TruncateWidth`, pinned by `TestFirstOutputLineKeepsMultibyteRunesIntact`.
152	Worth grepping for `[:` on strings when the remaining phases land.
153	
154	The two pinned tests that `t.Skip()`d became real assertions

gh pr create --base main --head docs/command-mode-key --title "docs: record the request for a command-mode key usable inside text fields" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
Adds §3.7 to `docs/backlog.md`.

**The request:** enter command mode with a modifier chord rather than a bare `:`, because the application is full of text inputs and inside one a `:` only inserts a colon.

**Why it is accurate:** `app.go:466` routes `:` through `maybeEnterInCommandMode`, which forwards the keystroke to the active input whenever `FormView.InEditMode()` is true. The `CommandModeView` escape hatch already exists for this, but its single implementation (`netdiag/update.go:18`) only fires on the topology tab in its ready state — where nothing is being edited anyway.

**The blocker, settled up front:** `ctrl+:` cannot be made to work. Ctrl only encodes ASCII `@`–`_` (0x40–0x5F); `:` is 0x3A, so the terminal sends a plain `:` or nothing. Reporting it needs the Kitty keyboard protocol or xterm `modifyOtherKeys`, and bubbletea v1.3.10 implements neither. A `case "ctrl+:"` would be dead code.

**What does work,** with the inventory of already-taken bindings: `alt+:` (bubbletea reports `alt+<rune>` from the ESC-prefix convention) or a free `ctrl+<letter>` — `ctrl+p` / `ctrl+g`, since `a c d e f k n o r s w y` are taken and `i m j h [` are Tab/Enter/LF/Backspace/Esc.

**Recommendation:** keep `:` and add one chord that always wins. It needs no `InEditMode()` check — `handleKeyMsg` sees every `tea.KeyMsg` before any view does.

Ripple mapped: the header prompt, `app_test.go:30`, every view's help per Rules 114/130/137, and `CommandModeView`, which becomes deletable.

## Test plan

- [x] Documentation only — no code changes.
EOF
)"

content.text:
J'ai mergé #15 d'abord, puis ajouté l'entrée en §3.7 du backlog : https://github.com/anthnel/devdesk/pull/16

**Ta remarque est exacte, et le code la concède déjà.** `app.go:466` fait passer `:` par `maybeEnterInCommandMode`, qui redirige la touche vers l'input actif dès que `FormView.InEditMode()` est vrai. Il existe même une échappatoire dédiée — l'interface `CommandModeView` — mais sa seule implémentation (`netdiag/update.go:18`) ne se déclenche que sur l'onglet topology en état ready, c'est-à-dire là où justement rien n'est en édition. Elle contourne un problème de routage, elle ne t'ouvre pas la porte pendant que tu tapes.

**En revanche `ctrl+:` précisément ne peut pas marcher**, et ça valait la peine de le trancher avant d'écrire une ligne. Un terminal encode Ctrl en effaçant des bits, ce qui ne couvre que l'ASCII `@`–`_` (0x40–0x5F). `:` vaut 0x3A : Ctrl+: envoie soit un `:` nu, soit rien. Le remonter comme touche distincte demande le protocole clavier Kitty ou `modifyOtherKeys` de xterm, et bubbletea v1.3.10 n'implémente ni l'un ni l'autre (aucune référence dans le module). Un `case "ctrl+:"` serait du code mort.

Ce qui marche, avec l'inventaire des bindings déjà pris :

| Option | Portabilité | Note |
|---|---|---|
| `alt+:` | bonne | bubbletea v1 remonte `alt+<rune>` via la convention préfixe ESC ; marche partout où « Alt sends Escape » est actif, le défaut quasi partout. Le plus proche de ta demande. |
| `ctrl+<lettre>` libre | totale | Pris : `a c d e f k n o r s w y`. `ctrl+i m j h [` sont Tab/Entrée/LF/Backspace/Esc, à ne pas toucher. Restent `b g l p t u v x z` — `ctrl+p` ou `ctrl+g` se lisent bien. |
| `esc` puis `:` | totale | Façon vim, mais `esc` veut déjà dire annuler/retour partout (Rule 111). Pas recommandé. |

Ma recommandation, notée comme telle dans l'entrée : **garder `:` et ajouter un chord qui gagne toujours**, plutôt que remplacer. La mémoire musculaire survit, et le nouveau binding n'a besoin d'aucune vérification `InEditMode()` — `handleKeyMsg` voit tous les `tea.KeyMsg` avant n'importe quelle vue, donc un `case` à cet endroit passe devant inconditionnellement. Trois lignes à côté du `case ":"` existant.

Le ripple est cartographié : le prompt du header (`app_header.go:56`), `app_test.go:30`, l'aide de chaque vue (Rules 114/130/137 — et trois vues ont déjà dérivé sur ce genre de changement), et `CommandModeView` qui devient supprimable une fois le nouveau binding en place.

Il te reste à choisir la touche — c'est la seule décision qui bloque l'implémentation.

Requested: enter command mode with a modifier chord rather than a bare `:`,
because the application is full of text inputs and inside one a `:` does nothing
but insert a colon.

The complaint is accurate and the current design concedes it. `internal/app/app.go:466`
routes `:` through `maybeEnterInCommandMode`, which asks the view whether it is
in edit mode (`FormView.InEditMode()`) and, if it is, forwards the keystroke to
the active input instead. So command mode is unreachable from any form, filter
box or search field — which is most of the application.

An escape hatch already exists and shows the shape of the problem: the
`CommandModeView` interface (`app.go:44`) lets a view declare that `:` should
enter command mode even while `InEditMode()` is true. Exactly one view
implements it — `internal/ui/netdiag/update.go:18` — and only for the topology
tab in its ready state, where nothing is being edited anyway. It papers over a
routing quirk; it does not give the user a way in while typing.

#### `ctrl+:` specifically cannot be made to work

Worth settling before any code is written. A terminal encodes Ctrl by clearing
bits, which only covers ASCII `@` through `_` (0x40–0x5F) plus a handful of
aliases. `:` is 0x3A and has no control encoding: pressing Ctrl+: sends either a
plain `:` or nothing at all. Reporting it as a distinct key needs the Kitty
keyboard protocol or xterm's `modifyOtherKeys`, and bubbletea v1.3.10 implements
neither — the module has no reference to either. A `case "ctrl+:"` would be dead
code.

#### What does work

| Option | Portability | Notes |

tab in its ready state, where nothing is being edited anyway. It papers over a
routing quirk; it does not give the user a way in while typing.

#### Worked example: the security view

`internal/ui/security/model.go:296` returns `InEditMode() == true` for focused
fields 1, 7 and 10 — target path, Trivy server, Gitleaks config. Field 7 is the
case that makes the point: its own placeholder is `https://trivy-server:4954`,
so the field has to accept **two** colons to hold a valid value. Forwarding `:`
to the input there is not a bug to fix; it is the only correct behaviour.

Which is exactly why `:` is the wrong key for command mode. The user's only
route out today is to move focus to a field that happens not to take text — a
checkbox — and press `:` there. Command-mode reachability ends up depending on
which control is focused, and nothing tells the user that.

`InEditMode()` is broader still: it is also true for `StateScanning`,
`StateResults` and `StateDetails`, and `m.confirmModal != nil`. In those states
there is no field to move focus to, so `:` is forwarded to the view, which has
no `case` for it and drops it silently — no view in the application handles `:`
itself. Reaching command mode from a results table means pressing `esc` to
leave the results first. That is the same defect as the text field, without
even a workaround.

content.text:
Exactement, et c'est le meilleur exemple possible — je l'ai ajouté à l'entrée (#16 mis à jour).

`internal/ui/security/model.go:296` renvoie `InEditMode() == true` pour les champs 1, 7 et 10 — target path, Trivy server, Gitleaks config. Le champ 7 est parlant parce que son propre placeholder est `https://trivy-server:4954` : il doit accepter **deux** `:` pour contenir une valeur valide. Rediriger `:` vers l'input là n'est pas un bug à corriger, c'est le seul comportement correct.

C'est précisément ce qui disqualifie `:` comme touche de mode commande. Ta seule sortie aujourd'hui, c'est de déplacer le focus sur un champ qui ne prend pas de texte — une checkbox — et de presser `:` là. La joignabilité du mode commande dépend donc du contrôle qui a le focus, et rien ne le signale à l'utilisateur.

Et c'est pire que ce que tu décris. `InEditMode()` est aussi vrai pour `StateScanning`, `StateResults`, `StateDetails` et quand une confirm modal est ouverte. Dans ces états **il n'y a aucun champ vers lequel déplacer le focus** : le `:` est transmis à la vue, qui n'a pas de `case` pour lui et le jette silencieusement — j'ai vérifié, aucune vue de l'application ne traite `:` elle-même. Depuis un tableau de résultats de scan, atteindre le mode commande impose de faire `esc` pour quitter les résultats d'abord. Même défaut, sans même le contournement.

Ça renforce la recommandation : le nouveau chord doit être intercepté dans `handleKeyMsg` **avant** le fork `InEditMode()`, sans condition. C'est ce qui le rend joignable depuis le champ Trivy server *et* depuis la table de résultats, alors que `CommandModeView` — qui essaie de résoudre ça vue par vue — ne peut couvrir ni l'un ni l'autre.

Du jargon de ma part, désolé — « chord » c'est simplement **une combinaison de touches pressées ensemble**, du type `ctrl+p` ou `alt+:`, par opposition à une touche seule comme `:`. Le terme vient du clavier de piano (plusieurs touches à la fois) et s'oppose à une *séquence* comme `esc` puis `:`, où on presse l'une après l'autre.

Donc « le nouveau chord » = la nouvelle combinaison qu'on choisira pour entrer en mode commande, quelle qu'elle soit : `alt+:`, `ctrl+p`, `ctrl+g`…

Le terme apparaît deux fois dans l'entrée du backlog (§3.7). Je peux le remplacer par « modifier combination », plus lisible, si tu préfères — dis-moi.

Et la décision qui reste bloquante, c'est laquelle de ces combinaisons tu veux :

| Candidat | Argument |
|---|---|
| `alt+:` | le plus proche de ta demande d'origine, garde le `:` dans le geste |
| `ctrl+p` | portabilité totale, aucun terminal exotique requis |
| `ctrl+g` | idem, et `g` est libre partout dans l'app |
